title: Daniel's Prayer and the Seventy Weeks
summary: Reading Jeremiah's prophecy that Jerusalem's desolation would last seventy years, Daniel turns to God in fasting and prays one of the Bible's great prayers of confession, pleading for the ruined city and sanctuary on the ground of God's mercy alone. While he is still praying, the angel Gabriel arrives with an answer: seventy weeks (usually understood as seventy sevens of years) are decreed for Jerusalem, ending in atonement and everlasting righteousness but passing through the cutting off of an anointed one and the destruction of the city.
story:
Chapters 7 and 8 showed Daniel empires rising and a fierce ruler attacking God's sanctuary, and chapter 8 ended with Daniel sick and bewildered. Chapter 9 turns from vision to Scripture and prayer. Babylon has just fallen to the Medes and Persians, and Daniel, now an old man who was carried off as a youth nearly seventy years before (1:1-6), realizes that the seventy years Jeremiah foretold are nearly complete. The exile is ending, but Daniel does not simply wait for it. He confesses the sin that caused it, taking his place among the guilty, and asks God to act for his own name.

God's answer widens his view. The return from Babylon, which Cyrus's decree will soon allow (Ezra 1:1-4), will not be the end of Israel's troubles. Jeremiah's seventy years become seventy weeks of years; the city will be rebuilt, but in times of distress, and an anointed one will be cut off and the city and sanctuary destroyed again before sin is finally dealt with. The rest of the book (chapters 10 to 12) fills in what those years will hold. This is the only chapter of Daniel that uses the covenant name of God, the LORD (YHWH), and it is the book's clearest bridge between the prophets who came before and the hope that looks beyond the return.
historical:
The chapter is dated to the first year of Darius son of Xerxes (Hebrew Ahasuerus), a Mede, the ruler the book places over Babylon after its fall in 539 BC (5:31). No Darius the Mede appears in Babylonian or Persian records, and the historical Xerxes I (486 to 465 BC) was the son, not the father, of Darius I. Proposals include Gubaru, the governor Cyrus installed over Babylon (John C. Whitcomb, Darius the Mede, 1959); Cyrus himself under another title, reading 6:28 as ‘Darius, that is, Cyrus’ (D. J. Wiseman); and, among critical scholars since H. H. Rowley (Darius the Mede and the Four World Empires, 1935), a literary figure shaped by the prophecies that the Medes would destroy Babylon (Isaiah 13:17; Jeremiah 51:11, 28). The year is about 539 or 538 BC. The Cyrus Cylinder, Cyrus's own clay account of his entry into Babylon, describes his return of displaced gods and peoples to their homes, the policy behind the decree allowing Jews to return and rebuild (Ezra 1:1-4; 6:3-5).

Daniel's starting point is Jeremiah, who had prophesied that the nations would serve the king of Babylon seventy years and that when “Babylon's seventy years are complete” God would bring his people home (Jeremiah 25:11-12; 29:10). Counted from Nebuchadnezzar's first move against Jerusalem in about 605 BC, when Daniel himself was taken (1:1), the seventy years reach close to Cyrus's decree in 539 or 538 BC; counted from the temple's destruction in 587 or 586 BC, they reach roughly to its rebuilding, completed in the sixth year of Darius I, 516 or 515 BC (Ezra 6:15). Zechariah 1:12 and 7:5, spoken in about 519 and 518 BC, still speak of seventy years of God's anger, and 2 Chronicles 36:21 connects the number with the sabbath years the land had been denied (Leviticus 26:34-35). Later biblical writers were already reading Jeremiah's number as a word that could be reckoned in more than one way.

The prophecy that answers Daniel is one of the most debated passages in the Bible, and its main readings are set out in the hard question below. Each locates its climax in a real crisis for Jerusalem and its temple. The first is the crisis under the Seleucid king Antiochus IV: the high priest Onias III was deposed and later murdered near Antioch around 171 BC (2 Maccabees 4:33-35); Antiochus plundered the temple in 169 BC; and on the fifteenth of Kislev in 167 BC his officials set up on the altar what 1 Maccabees 1:54 calls, in the very words of the Greek Daniel, an abomination of desolation, rededicating the temple to Olympian Zeus (2 Maccabees 6:2). The temple was cleansed and rededicated in Kislev 164 BC (1 Maccabees 4:52-54), the origin of Hanukkah. The second is the ministry and death of Jesus in the early first century AD and the Roman destruction of the city and temple in AD 70, which Josephus describes in the sixth book of his Jewish War. The third, in dispensational readings, is a final crisis still to come.

The prayer itself has close relatives in the literature of the period. Baruch 1:15 to 2:19, in the Greek Old Testament and the Apocrypha, follows Daniel's prayer phrase by phrase, beginning with the same contrast of righteousness belonging to God and shame to us; scholars debate which depends on which, or whether both draw on a shared liturgical prayer. Among the Dead Sea Scrolls, the Words of the Luminaries (4Q504) preserves weekday prayers of communal confession of the same kind, and 11QMelchizedek (11Q13) identifies the herald of good news in Isaiah 52:7 with ‘the anointed of the spirit’ of whom Daniel spoke, and expects atonement at the end of ten jubilees, that is, 490 years.
cultural:
Daniel prays with fasting, sackcloth, and ashes, the standard signs of mourning and repentance in Israel and its neighbors: coarse goat-hair cloth worn against the skin, ashes or dust on the head, food refused (compare Nehemiah 9:1; Esther 4:1-3; Jonah 3:5-8). These were not ways of earning a hearing but bodily ways of agreeing with God's verdict and humbling oneself before him. His prayer draws heavily on Deuteronomy and on Solomon's prayer at the dedication of the temple, which asked God to hear exiles who came to their senses in the land of their captors and prayed toward the land, the city, and the house built for his name, confessing, “We have sinned and done wrong; we have acted wickedly” (1 Kings 8:47). Daniel uses nearly those words (verse 5), and he had kept Solomon's practice of praying toward Jerusalem three times a day (6:10).

Gabriel arrives about the time of the evening sacrifice (verse 21), although the temple had lain in ruins for nearly fifty years. The evening offering (minchat erev) was offered in the late afternoon (Exodus 29:38-42); Josephus says the priests offered the daily sacrifices in the morning and about the ninth hour, around three in the afternoon (Antiquities 14.65). It became a set hour of prayer: Ezra prayed at it (Ezra 9:5), Psalm 141:2 compares prayer to it, and in Acts Peter and John go up to the temple at the ninth hour, the hour of prayer (Acts 3:1). The old rhythm of temple worship still shaped the prayer life of the exiles, and later Jewish tradition traced the three daily prayers of the synagogue to the times of the temple offerings.

The prayer's logic is the covenant's logic. Moses had warned that disobedience would bring curses, including defeat and exile (Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 28), and had promised that when the people confessed their iniquity and that of their fathers, God would remember his covenant (Leviticus 26:40-45; Deuteronomy 30:1-5). When Daniel says “the oath and the curse written in the Law of Moses” has been poured out (verse 11), he is not complaining; he is agreeing with God's verdict and appealing to the same Law's promise. Prayers of this kind, communal confessions spoken by a leader on behalf of the people, also appear in Ezra 9:6-15, Nehemiah 1:5-11 and 9:6-37, and they became a pattern for later Jewish penitential prayer. Such a leader confesses in the first person plural even when he had not shared in the sins, because the covenant bound the generations together; Leviticus 26:40 names the sins of the fathers alongside the people's own.

The numbers of Gabriel's answer draw on Israel's calendar of sevens. Every seventh year was a sabbath for the land (Leviticus 25:1-7), and after seven sevens of years came the jubilee, when debts were released and land returned to its families (Leviticus 25:8-12). Seventy sevens of years is 490 years, ten jubilees, a period in which a small sabbath pattern is magnified into a great release. Readers in the ancient world knew these cycles, which is why the scroll from Qumran could reckon the end in jubilees.
literary:
The chapter has three parts: Daniel's reading of Scripture (verses 1 to 3), his prayer (verses 4 to 19), and Gabriel's answer (verses 20 to 27). It is the one chapter in the book built around a written text: Daniel understands ‘from the books’ (verse 2), the prayer echoes the Law of Moses and the prophets, and the answer reinterprets a prophecy already given.

The prayer is carefully built. It opens with an invocation drawn from Deuteronomy 7:9 and used again in Nehemiah 1:5, addressing “the great and awesome God, who keeps His covenant of loving devotion to those who love Him and keep His commandments” (verse 4). A long confession follows (verses 5 to 14), in which the verbs pile up (sinned, done wrong, acted wickedly, rebelled, turned away) and the refrain is contrast: to God belong righteousness (verse 7) and compassion and forgiveness (verse 9); to us, shame. The confession ends by declaring God righteous in all he has done (verse 14). Then the prayer turns (‘and now’, verse 15) to petition, recalling the exodus and rising in urgency to a climax in verse 19, a string of short imperatives: “O Lord, listen! O Lord, forgive! O Lord, hear and act!” As it rises, the possessive pronouns shift from ‘our’ to ‘your’: your city, your holy mountain, your desolate sanctuary, the city that bears your name, your people. The request rests entirely on God's own character and name: “we are not presenting our petitions before You because of our righteous acts, but because of Your great compassion” (verse 18). The divine name YHWH, rendered LORD, occurs eight times in this chapter and nowhere else in Daniel, and the prayer's Hebrew is smoother and more traditional than the rest of the book, which leads some scholars to think Daniel is quoting or adapting a known liturgical prayer.

Gabriel's answer (verses 24 to 27) is compressed and allusive poetry, built on a play with sevens: Jeremiah's seventy years become seventy weeks, divided into seven, sixty-two, and one. Verse 24 lists six purposes as six infinitives, often read as three pairs, three dealing with sin (to stop transgression, end sin, atone for iniquity) and three with what God will bring (everlasting righteousness, the sealing of vision and prophet, the anointing of a most holy place or person). Verses 25 to 27 then walk through the periods, and the language turns dark: an anointed one cut off, a prince whose people destroy, a flood, war, desolations, and an abomination. The chapter ends not with the fulfillment of the six purposes but with decreed destruction poured out on the desolator, leaving the reader, like Daniel, to hold the promise and the pain together.

outline.t: Daniel reads Jeremiah and turns to prayer
Confession: God is righteous, and we have sinned
Petition: for your sake, restore your city
Gabriel comes while Daniel is still praying

doctrines.note: Daniel's prayer is shaped by Scripture, begins with God's character, confesses sin honestly, and appeals to God's mercy and reputation. Knowing that God had promised restoration did not make Daniel passive; it moved him to pray for what God had promised. The answer comes ‘at the beginning of your petitions’ (verse 23), which shows God hearing before the prayer is finished, not being persuaded by its length.

Daniel had lived faithfully, yet he confesses Israel's sin as his own: “we have sinned and done wrong” (verse 5). Biblical repentance includes agreeing with God's judgment, taking responsibility for the sins of one's community and not only one's private failings, and turning to God's compassion rather than one's own record.

The chapter reads the exile as covenant curse, the oath written in the Law of Moses poured out (verse 11), and it reads the promised return through Jeremiah's seventy years. Gabriel's answer teaches that return to the land is not the same as the end of exile: the deeper problem of sin remains until God deals with it.

Gabriel's six purposes for the seventy weeks include putting “an end to sin” and making “atonement for iniquity” (verse 24), using kipper, the verb of Israel's sacrifices and the Day of Atonement. Return from exile will not solve the problem that caused it; God himself must deal with sin and bring in everlasting righteousness.

Verses 25 and 26 speak of an anointed one, a prince, who will be cut off. Christians have long read this as a prophecy of Jesus, while Jewish and critical interpreters identify the figure with Cyrus, a high priest such as Joshua or Onias III, or a later king; the options are set out in the hard question below.

words.note: Shavua, a week, literally a unit of seven. The noun occurs about twenty times, usually for the seven-day week and the Festival of Weeks, and eight times in Daniel (9:24-27; 10:2-3). In 10:2-3 Daniel specifies ‘weeks of days’, which suggests that the unqualified weeks here are something else, almost certainly weeks of years, so that seventy weeks equals 490 years, Jeremiah's seventy multiplied by seven. The pattern echoes the sabbatical year and the Jubilee (Leviticus 25), and the exile itself was linked to the land's unkept sabbaths (2 Chronicles 36:21). Whether the numbers are exact chronology or symbolic periods is the central question of the chapter.

Mashiach, anointed one, the word behind Messiah and, through Greek, Christ. It occurs about thirty-nine times in the Old Testament, for anointed priests (Leviticus 4:3), for Saul and David and their successors as ‘the LORD's anointed’, and once for the Persian Cyrus (Isaiah 45:1). In verses 25 and 26 the Hebrew has no article, so it can be read as ‘an anointed one’, a leader, rather than the title ‘the Messiah’, which as a fixed title is rare before the late Second Temple period. Translations that capitalize it, as the BSB does, reflect the Christian reading.

Nagid, leader, ruler, prince. It occurs about forty-four times, often for one designated by God to lead, as Saul and David were anointed nagid over Israel (1 Samuel 9:16; 2 Samuel 5:2), but also for temple officers (1 Chronicles 9:11) and foreign rulers (Ezekiel 28:2). It appears in verse 25 with the anointed one and in verse 26 for the prince who is to come, whose people destroy the city. The same title for two figures, one to be cut off and one who destroys, is part of what makes the passage so contested.

Kipper, to atone, cover, make propitiation, occurs about a hundred times, mostly in Leviticus and Numbers for the priest's work at the altar and on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16). Scholars debate whether its root sense is ‘cover’ or ‘wipe away’, but its usage matters more than its origin: it names the removal of guilt so that God's people may live in his presence. Its appearance among the purposes of the seventy weeks (verse 24) shows that the end God intends is not only political restoration but the removal of sin.

Yadah, in its reflexive stem (hitpael) to confess, acknowledge. The verb occurs over a hundred times, mostly in the causative stem meaning to praise or give thanks, and the confessing sense appears only about a dozen times, in Leviticus (5:5; 16:21; 26:40), Ezra 10:1, Nehemiah 1:6 and 9:2-3, and here (verses 4 and 20). The overlap is instructive: to confess sin and to praise God are both ways of acknowledging the truth about God, and Daniel's confession begins and ends in praise of God's righteousness and compassion.

Rachamim, compassion, mercy, a plural noun related to rechem, womb. It occurs about thirty-nine times and names the tender, visceral mercy of a parent. In verses 9 and 18 it is the ground of Daniel's appeal: to the Lord belong compassion and forgiveness, and the people ask ‘because of Your great compassion’, not their righteousness. The phrase ‘great compassion’ recalls David's choice to fall into God's hands rather than man's (2 Samuel 24:14).

Chesed, loyal love, covenant faithfulness, which the BSB renders loving devotion. It occurs about 250 times, and it is the quality God proclaims as his own in Exodus 34:6-7. Daniel's prayer opens by confessing that God keeps his covenant of loving devotion (verse 4). The whole appeal rests on it: Israel has broken the covenant, but God's steadfast loyalty is the ground on which Daniel dares to ask.

Shiqquts, an abomination, a detestable thing. It occurs about twenty-eight times, almost always for idols and the objects of pagan worship (1 Kings 11:5, 7; 2 Kings 23:13). Joined with a form of shamem, to be desolate or appalled, it becomes the abomination that causes desolation (verse 27; also 11:31 and 12:11), a byword for the desecration of God's sanctuary. Eberhard Nestle proposed in 1884 that the phrase mocks the title of the Syrian god Baal Shamem, ‘lord of heaven’. Jesus used the phrase for the coming destruction of the temple (Matthew 24:15; Mark 13:14).

christ:
Christians from the second century onward have read verses 24 to 27 as pointing to Jesus: an anointed one who comes after sixty-nine weeks, is cut off and has nothing, and after whom the city and sanctuary are destroyed, as happened in AD 70. On that reading the purposes of verse 24, to put an end to sin, make atonement for iniquity, and bring in everlasting righteousness, are what Christ accomplished by his death and resurrection. Hebrews says that Christ has appeared once for all at the end of the ages to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself (Hebrews 9:26), and after quoting Jeremiah's promise of forgiveness it concludes that “an offering for sin is no longer needed” (Hebrews 10:18), which many have heard as the fulfillment of sacrifice and offering brought to an end in the middle of the week (verse 27). Some interpreters also read ‘to anoint the Most Holy’ as the anointing of Jesus with the Spirit (Luke 4:18; Acts 10:38), though most take it of a sanctuary.

Not all interpreters agree that the passage predicts Jesus specifically, and the arithmetic is disputed, as the hard question explains. But even on other readings the chapter's direction points toward the gospel. Israel's deepest need is not return from exile but atonement; the need is met by God's compassion, not human merit; and the righteousness God brings is everlasting. The New Testament sees that pattern completed in Christ, the righteous one who takes the place of the unrighteous, much as Daniel, the righteous man, took his place among the guilty in confession.

Jesus himself took up the chapter's phrase when he warned of Jerusalem's coming fall: “So when you see standing in the holy place ‘the abomination of desolation,’ described by the prophet Daniel (let the reader understand)” (Matthew 24:15). Luke's parallel speaks of Jerusalem surrounded by armies (Luke 21:20), and the Roman siege of AD 66 to 70 is the event most readers see in his warning. Gabriel, who appears in the Old Testament only in Daniel 8 and 9, next appears in Luke 1, at the hour of incense in the temple, announcing the births of John and of Jesus (Luke 1:19, 26). The messenger who told Daniel that the answer to Israel's sin lay further off than he thought is the one who announces that it has arrived.
interpretation:
Jewish readers engaged the seventy weeks early. 11QMelchizedek from Qumran reckons the end in ten jubilees and links Daniel's anointed one to the herald of Isaiah 52:7, and Josephus praised Daniel as a prophet who fixed the time of the events he foretold (Antiquities 10.267). The rabbinic chronicle Seder Olam Rabbah, attributed to Yose ben Halafta in the second century, counts the 490 years as seventy years of exile and 420 years of the Second Temple ending in AD 70, a reckoning the Talmud assumes (Nazir 32b). Rashi identified the anointed prince of verse 25 with Cyrus and the anointed one cut off with Agrippa, the last Jewish king. The Talmud also warns against those who calculate the end (Sanhedrin 97b), a caution Maimonides repeated in his Epistle to Yemen (about 1172), though Isaac Abravanel, writing after the expulsion from Spain, built his Ma'yenei ha-Yeshu'ah (1496) around Daniel's reckonings. Daniel's prayer entered Jewish worship: the preliminary morning prayer Master of All Worlds borrows verse 18, the long supplications said on Monday and Thursday mornings take up the cry of verse 19, and the cry of verse 19 is said in the penitential Selichot before the High Holy Days.

Among Christians, Tertullian (Against the Jews 8, about 200) and Clement of Alexandria counted the weeks to Christ and the fall of Jerusalem, and Julius Africanus, in fragments of his Chronography preserved by Eusebius, counted them from the twentieth year of Artaxerxes using lunar years. Jerome's Commentary on Daniel (about 407) set out the views of Africanus, Eusebius, Hippolytus, Apollinaris, Clement, Origen, and Tertullian and declined to choose among them. Calvin's lectures on Daniel (1561) took Christ as the one who confirms the covenant in the final week. Isaac Newton wrote on the weeks in his Observations upon the Prophecies of Daniel (1733), and Sir Robert Anderson's The Coming Prince argued for 173,880 days of 360-day years from 445 BC to the triumphal entry, a scheme refined by Harold Hoehner (Chronological Aspects of the Life of Christ, 1977) and influential in dispensational teaching through the Scofield Reference Bible. James Montgomery (International Critical Commentary, 1927) and John Collins (Hermeneia, 1993) gave the critical reading its standard form.
text:
Several differences between English Bibles in this chapter come from the Hebrew and the ancient versions. The verse numbers are the same in Hebrew and English.

Verse 25 is the most consequential. The Masoretes, the medieval scribes who fixed the pointing and accents of the Hebrew text, placed their main dividing accent (the atnach) after ‘seven weeks’. Followed strictly, the verse reads ‘until an anointed prince, seven weeks; and for sixty-two weeks it shall be rebuilt’, so that the anointed one arrives after forty-nine years; the RSV, NRSV, ESV, and the Jewish Publication Society version follow the accent. The KJV, NASB, NIV, and BSB join the numbers, “seven weeks and sixty-two weeks”, so that he arrives after 483 years. They note that the accents are a later reading tradition, not part of the consonantal text, and that Theodotion's Greek, the version the church used, also joins the numbers. Jewish polemicists have argued that the Christian punctuation disregards the text; Christian scholars answer that the accents are themselves an interpretation.

In verse 24 the written consonants (Ketiv) and the reading tradition (Qere) differ twice: the consonants suggest ‘to restrain’ transgression and ‘to seal up’ sins, the reading ‘to finish’ transgression and ‘to complete’ sin; English translations follow the reading. In verse 26 the phrase “will have nothing” renders two Hebrew words, ‘and there is not to him’, which the KJV took as ‘but not for himself’ and others as ‘and shall have no one’ or ‘and shall have nothing’. In verse 27 the Hebrew has no word for temple; ‘on the wing of abominations’ is the literal sense, and the phrase “on the wing of the temple” blends the Hebrew with the Greek versions, which read ‘upon the temple’. In verse 21 the words rendered ‘in swift flight’ come from a root meaning to fly but resemble one meaning to be weary, and some translations say Gabriel came to Daniel when he was exhausted. The Old Greek of verses 24 to 27 differs so sharply from the Hebrew that some scholars think it reflects a translator already reading the passage as a history of the Maccabean crisis.

teach.big: God's promises do not make his people passive; they drive them to honest confession and bold prayer, and God answers by revealing that his final remedy for sin lies beyond anything the return from exile could supply.

outline.t: Faithful prayer begins with reading Scripture and taking God's promises seriously enough to plead for them.
True confession starts with who God is, names sin plainly, includes ourselves in our people's guilt, and agrees that God is right.
Bold petition rests on God's compassion and his name, never on our record, and it asks God to act for his own sake.
God hears from the first word, and he answers the humble with understanding and the assurance that they are precious to him.
God has set a limit to Jerusalem's suffering and a goal beyond it: sin ended, atonement made, righteousness brought in, even though the road leads through the cutting off of an anointed one.

teach.pitfalls:
The first pitfall is to spend the whole lesson on the arithmetic of verses 24 to 27 and skip the prayer, which takes up most of the chapter and is the part every reader can practice. The seventy weeks deserve careful treatment, but a teacher who presents only one scheme of dates as certain misleads the room; faithful interpreters disagree, and the options should be laid out fairly. A second pitfall is date-setting. The chapter has been used for centuries to calculate the end, and the Talmud's warning against calculating the end is worth hearing: the passage assures God's people that history is bounded and purposeful, not that its calendar can be mastered.

A third pitfall treats Daniel's confession as a model of self-hatred. Daniel names sin plainly, but his prayer is full of confidence in God's compassion and ends in urgent hope. A fourth ignores the corporate dimension, turning the prayer into individual devotion alone; Daniel confesses the sins of kings, leaders, fathers, and people, and his prayer is a model for praying about a church or nation's sins in which the one praying is included. Finally, avoid using verse 23, ‘you are highly precious’, as if God answered Daniel because he was precious; the answer went out at the beginning of the prayer, and the prayer itself disclaims any appeal to merit.
teach.pastoral: The prayer will press on people who carry shame, whether for their own sins or for the sins of their family, church, or nation. It shows that shame can be spoken honestly before God without despair, because the prayer's ground is God's compassion. For the scrupulous, notice that Daniel confesses once, fully, and then turns to petition; confession is not meant to be endless. For those grieving institutional failures, such as abuse in a church, the prayer offers words for owning a community's sin without excusing it. Be careful not to imply that victims share the guilt of what was done to them; Daniel confesses the sins of those who ruled and failed, and a victim is not the one who needs to repent.

hard.q: What are the seventy weeks, and who is the anointed one who is cut off?
hard.a:
The strongest objections to the traditional Christian reading come from two directions. Jewish interpreters have argued that the passage concerns the Second Temple and its fall, not the Messiah: Seder Olam Rabbah counts seventy years of exile and 420 years to AD 70, and Rashi identified the anointed prince with Cyrus and the anointed one cut off with Agrippa. They add that the Hebrew has no article (‘an anointed one’, not ‘the Messiah’), and that joining the seven and sixty-two weeks overrides the Masoretic accent. Critical scholars, following Porphyry in antiquity and James Montgomery (1927) and John Collins (1993) in modern times, read the weeks against the second century BC. The seven weeks run from Jeremiah's word (about 587 BC) to an anointed leader after the exile, Cyrus or the high priest Joshua; the anointed one cut off after sixty-two more weeks is the high priest Onias III, murdered around 171 BC; and the prince who is to come is Antiochus IV, whose desecration of the temple in 167 BC falls in the middle of the last week. Defenders of this reading grant that the numbers do not add up exactly and treat them as schematic, as other ancient chronologies did.

The traditional messianic reading, held by many church fathers, by Calvin, and by interpreters such as E. J. Young (The Prophecy of Daniel, 1949), counts sixty-nine weeks from a Persian decree to restore Jerusalem to the time of Jesus in the early first century AD. Starting points differ: Cyrus's decree of 539 or 538 BC, read symbolically, or Artaxerxes' commission to Ezra in about 458 or 457 BC, which with 483 years reaches about AD 26 or 27, near the start of Jesus' ministry. The anointed one cut off is Christ crucified; the people of the prince who destroy the city are the Romans of AD 70; and the one who confirms a covenant for one week is often read as Christ, whose death ends sacrifice. Its strength is that it explains the large purposes of verse 24; its difficulties are the choice of a starting point and the gap of some forty years between the cross and AD 70.

The dispensational reading, influential among many evangelicals since the nineteenth century, agrees that the sixty-nine weeks end with the Messiah, often counted from Artaxerxes' decree to Nehemiah in 445 or 444 BC using years of 360 days (Sir Robert Anderson; Harold Hoehner). It sees a gap between the sixty-ninth and seventieth weeks covering the present age, and places the seventieth week in the future, when a coming ruler will make a seven-year covenant and break it halfway through. It keeps the numbers literal but must posit a gap the text does not mention. A fourth, symbolic reading, found in C. F. Keil's nineteenth-century commentary and in some later Reformed writers, takes the periods as sacred measures rather than calendar years, running from the return to the end of history.

Each reading has real strengths and real difficulties, and Jerome, having set out the views of the fathers, refused to choose among them. Faithful readers differ here, and this remains a second-order question. The chapter's main point, that God has set a limit to his people's suffering and will finally deal with sin, stands on each.

observe: What does Daniel read in verse 2, and what does he do about it in verse 3?
List the things Daniel says belong to God and the things he says belong to ‘us’ in verses 7 to 9. What contrast does the prayer draw?
What six things are the seventy weeks decreed to accomplish in verse 24?
interpret: Daniel knew that God had promised the exile would end. Why did that promise lead him to confession and prayer rather than simply waiting?
Why does Daniel say ‘we have sinned’ when the book presents him as faithful? What does that suggest about how the covenant bound a people together?
What does Gabriel's answer suggest about the difference between returning to the land and the end of the exile's deeper cause?
apply: Daniel's prayer rests entirely on God's compassion and name, not on anyone's righteousness. What would change in your prayers if you asked on that ground alone?
Is there a sin of your family, church, or nation that you have never brought before God? How could Daniel's prayer give you words for it?
The answer went out at the beginning of Daniel's prayer. How does that affect the way you think about unanswered or long prayers?
